title: The face of truth, covered in gold
hookLine: an old warrior waits for the sun, and the Isha ends with a prayer for the last walk
carry: uncover it, so I may see

cards: At the end of the great war, the old warrior Bhishma lies on a bed of arrows.
He has the gift of choosing when he dies, and the Mahabharata says he chooses to wait for the sun to turn north, the season held most auspicious for leaving the body.
Fifty-eight nights he lies there, teaching the Pandavas, and watching the sun. A dying man, waiting for light. The Isha ends at that kind of moment.
After a week of teaching, it stops explaining, turns to the sun, and prays.

teach.h: THE FACE OF TRUTH, COVERED WITH GOLD.
teach.b: Verse fifteen: hiranmayena patrena satyasyapihitam mukham. The face of truth is covered with a golden disc, like a lid.

teach.h: UNCOVER IT, SO I MAY SEE.
teach.b: The speaker turns to Pushan, the nourisher, a name for the sun: uncover it, so that I, whose way is truth, may see. Notice the lid isn't ugly. It's gold.
What hides the truth is often something lovely: praise, comfort, the shine of what we own. Verse sixteen: spread out your rays, gather in your light, so I can see your most blessed form.

Then a startling line: that person there, I am he. The one behind the gold isn't a stranger. Verse seventeen is spoken at the edge of death: the breath goes back to the immortal wind, and this body ends in ashes.
Om, mind, remember; remember what was done.

teach.h: AGNI: LEAD US BY THE GOOD PATH.
teach.b: And verse eighteen turns to Agni, fire: lead us by the good path, you who know all our ways; take the crooked wrong away from us. This is how Hinduism meets a death: with a prayer to be led.
Some families say these verses at a bedside, and at the cremation the body is given to Agni, the fire this verse asks for guidance. And remember who gave Yajnavalkya this Veda: the sun.
The week began with the sun's gift and ends with a prayer to it. All this is the Lord's. Renounce, and enjoy.
Work, offered. Far, and near. One self in every being.
Knowing and doing. Uncover it, so I may see.

how: Isha verses 15–18 are recited at some Hindu funerals and at the bedside of the dying; verse 18, the prayer to Agni to lead by the good path, also appears in the Rig Veda (1.189.1).

games.q: the last four verses — tap the pairs.
p: spoken at the edge of death
fire: lead us by the good path

s: the Isha pictures truth hidden behind something ugly
behind gold: the face of truth is covered with a golden disc.
the last verses of the Isha are said at some Hindu bedsides and funerals
the breath to the wind, the body to ashes, and the prayer to Agni.
verse sixteen says the one hidden behind the gold is a stranger
it says: that person there, I am he.

games.q: truth is hidden behind a golden lid. what does the speaker do?
o: ask the sun to uncover it.
decide the gold is the truth.
games.why: he asks Pushan, the sun, to uncover it, so the one whose way is truth may see.

practice: Ask yourself what the golden lid in your life is right now: something good, even lovely, that might be keeping you from seeing what's true; you don't have to remove it, just name it quietly.

Then breathe, and on each out-breath imagine the lid lifting a little. If you pray, you can say the verse's own request in your own language, uncover it, so I may see; otherwise, just watch the breath.

wordCard.voice: Hiranmaya, golden, made of gold. The face of truth is covered with a golden disc; Pushan, the sun, is asked to uncover it, so the truthful may see.

orig.note: Sanskrit: hiranmaya, golden, made of gold; verse 15: the face of truth covered with a golden disc.

carryVoice: Your line: uncover it, so I may see. Tomorrow, a new Upanishad that starts with a child's question. That's the whole Isha, and day two hundred thirty-eight.
